```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(knowledgelayer)
root <- file.path(tempdir(), "office")
unlink(root, recursive = TRUE)
```

A reproducible analytical pipeline (RAP: code that takes raw data all the
way to the published output, with no manual steps) answers *how was this
number made?* It does not answer *what else in this office touches the same
data*, *who could run this if its author were out tomorrow*, or *who decided
to exclude those records, and on what basis*. Those answers usually live in
people's heads.

This package keeps them in plain files beside the code. That collection of
files is what it calls a **knowledge layer**: the office's record of its
projects, how they connect, who holds them, and what was decided.

Nothing here needs a server, a database or a version control system. Every
file is text that a person can read and a diff tool can compare, so the layer
works on a shared drive today and moves into version control unchanged later.

For a shorter, step-by-step walkthrough, open the runbook with `kl_runbook()`;
it links to a sample review page you can click around in. The README, on the
package's source page, covers installing and what IT needs.

Every function takes a `path` to the folder holding the layer. Set it once
instead:

```{r}
kl_init(root)
options(knowledgelayer.path = root)
```

## 1. Register the work, and connect it

```{r}
kl_add_project("annual-2025", "Annual performance report 2025",
               owner = "Analyst A", status = "done",
               sources = "Case management extract", methods = "targets pipeline")
kl_add_project("annual-2026", "Annual performance report 2026",
               owner = "Analyst A",
               sources = c("Case management extract", "Complaint intake records"),
               methods = c("targets pipeline", "text matching on complaint narratives"),
               location = "S:/Analytics/annual-2026")
kl_add_project("mentorship-survey", "Mentorship survey analysis",
               owner = "Analyst B", people = c("Analyst B", "Analyst C"),
               sources = "Survey platform export")

kl_link("annual-2026", "annual-2025", "reuses-code-from")
kl_link("mentorship-survey", "annual-2026", "shares-method-with",
        note = "same demographic join")

kl_projects()[, c("id", "owner", "n_people", "status")]
```

Before starting anything new, search what the office already knows:

```{r}
kl_find("complaint")[, c("id", "title", "owner")]
```

## 2. Find the single points of knowledge

A **single point of knowledge** is work that only one person could run or
explain. If they are out, it stops.

```{r}
kl_single_points()
```

## 3. Keep a board, so ideas are written down without being promised

Every project collects "we should also..." ideas. Put them in the Inbox the
moment they come up; nothing reaches the Roadmap until a person triages it.
Parking says "not now" without saying "never".

```{r}
i1 <- kl_inbox("Add district-level rates", "annual-2026", by = "Supervisor S")
i2 <- kl_inbox("Rewrite the cleaning step in data.table", "annual-2026")
i3 <- kl_inbox("Interactive map of complaint density", "annual-2026")
kl_triage(c(i1, i2, i3), c("TAKE", "HOLD", "DROP"), by = "Analyst A",
          reasons = c("", "after the report ships", "outside this report's remit"))
kl_roadmap_status(i1, "doing")
kl_board("annual-2026")
```

A dropped idea goes into the decision log, so it is not argued again from
scratch next year. "Done" requires saying how you know it works.

## 4. Write the handoff before you need it

The fix for a single point of knowledge is a written handoff.
`kl_handoff()` drafts one from what the layer already knows (sources,
links, decisions, the board) and marks what only the author can add. The
section that matters most is *decisions and why*: what was done is easy to
rebuild, but why it was done is what gets lost.

```{r}
note <- kl_handoff("annual-2026")
cat(readLines(note), sep = "\n")
```

## 5. Measure what your jurisdiction's data infrastructure offers

One of the usual barriers to adopting reproducible pipelines is not skill
but supply: clean, machine-readable data to point them at. That is worth
measuring, because it tells an oversight office what it can automate today
and what it will have to request, build or recommend.

The UK, where reproducible analytical pipelines began, also has a model for
the supply side. The Local Government Association runs LG Inform Plus, a
shared data, standards and benchmarking service for English councils. Its
catalog of capabilities makes a good checklist: for each thing it offers,
does a local tool deliver it here?

```{r}
cl <- kl_checklist()
table(cl$theme, cl$kind)
```

The 22 *capabilities* are things a service does (a records-retention
register, an open-data API, a benchmarking club). The 15 *patterns* are
design habits that recur across them (identifiers in web addresses,
versioned changelogs, public by default). The rows are written in UK
local-government language; `kl_uk_terms()` translates it:

```{r}
head(kl_uk_terms()[, c("term", "us_nearest")], 8)
```

### Fit it to your city

1. **Choose your rows.** Not every row matters to an oversight office.
   Records retention, statutory mandates, data provenance and open-data
   access usually do; a council's internal publishing tools may not. Drop the
   rest, so the matrix measures what your office would act on.
2. **Translate as you go.** Read each row with `kl_uk_terms()` open. Where
   the US has no close equivalent, keep the row: an absence can be the
   finding.
3. **Add your own rows** for local sources the UK model doesn't have:
   ```r
   mine <- data.frame(id = "cap-complaint-narratives", kind = "capability",
                      theme = "data-and-reports",
                      capability = "Searchable complaint narratives, available to oversight",
                      uk_tool = "", uk_status = "")
   city <- kl_coverage_new("Example City", checklist = rbind(kl_checklist(), mine))
   ```
4. **Rate only what you have checked,** with dated evidence a reader can
   follow. Every row begins *unassessed*, which is different from *missing*:
   one makes no claim, the other is a finding.
5. **Be fair to the owner.** A `missing` or `stub` is a statement about
   another agency's systems. Say specifically what is absent, and check it
   with the agency that runs the system before the matrix goes beyond your
   office.
6. **Check it, then date it.** Run `kl_coverage_check()` before sharing, and
   recheck yearly: systems change, and every rating carries the date it was
   true.

A worked start, for an invented city. The tools, gaps and evidence below are
illustrative only, not a rating of any real place:

```{r}
city <- kl_coverage_new("Example City")
city <- kl_coverage_set(city, "cap-api-open-data", tool = "Example City data portal",
                        status = "stub",
                        evidence = "Illustrative: the portal's published API documentation",
                        gap = "Illustrative: datasets have an API, with no shared standards lists behind them")
city <- kl_coverage_set(city, "pat-12-versioned-changelog", status = "missing",
                        evidence = "Illustrative: the pages of five high-use datasets",
                        gap = "Illustrative: no public changelog on the datasets checked")
kl_coverage_check(city)
kl_coverage_summary(city, by = "kind")
```

## 6. Review findings without rubber-stamping them

Independent review is where an office's credibility is made. The weak point
is the review that happens in someone's inbox: "looks good" leaves no record
of what was actually decided. Here, findings go onto a review page, each with
a proposed verdict, and the reviewer's export becomes the record.

Findings come from your existing review template, and from reading the
report the way its harshest reader will:

```{r}
kl_review_angles()$angle
```

Propose the verdict you would stand behind for each finding, or `DISCUSS`
if you cannot. You cannot propose `TWEAK`: it means "yes, but my way", and
only the reviewer's note can say what that way is.

```{r}
findings <- kl_findings(
  id = c("F1", "F2", "F3"),
  finding = c("312 records appear twice after the address join",
              "Chart 3 labels the 2025 series as 2024",
              "Rate in table 2 uses records, not population, as denominator"),
  severity = c("high", "low", "high"),
  proposed_fix = c("Deduplicate on record id before the join",
                   "Fix the label in the plot function",
                   "Recompute per 100,000 residents"),
  source = "independent review checklist")

dir.create(file.path(root, "qa"))
kl_write_findings(findings, file.path(root, "qa", "findings.csv"))

kl_review_page(findings, file.path(root, "qa", "REVIEW_annual-2026-qa.html"),
               review_id = "annual-2026-qa",
               title = "Annual report 2026: independent review",
               author = "Analyst A", return_to = "Analyst A")
```

Email the page to the reviewer. They save it, open it in a browser, rule on
each finding and export `APPROVED_annual-2026-qa_<date>.json`, which they
send back. The page tells them all of this, and saves their work in the
browser as they go. Back in R:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
v <- kl_read_verdicts(kl_newest_verdicts(file.path(root, "qa"), review = "annual-2026-qa"))
kl_rubber_stamp_check(v, findings)
```

The check flags the marks of a review that did not happen: every proposal
accepted with no notes, findings never on screen long enough to read, a
high-severity finding waved through without comment, an author reviewing
their own work. It refuses an export that leaves any finding undecided,
one made on findings that have since changed, and a `TWEAK` with no note,
because a tweak without a note gives no instruction.

## 7. Let the review gate the pipeline

In a `targets` pipeline, make the report depend on the gate, so it cannot
build until the review is in and has passed:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tar_option_set(packages = "knowledgelayer")

list(
  tar_target(findings_file, "qa/findings.csv", format = "file"),
  tar_target(findings, kl_read_findings(findings_file)),
  tar_target(verdict_file, kl_newest_verdicts("qa", review = "annual-2026-qa"), format = "file"),
  tar_target(cleared, kl_gate(verdict_file, findings)),
  tar_target(report, render_report(cleaned_data, cleared))
)
```

`kl_gate()` stops with an error if the review failed, and returns only the
findings cleared for action, with the reviewer's note as the instruction for
any `TWEAK`. Record the review in the decision log once, outside the
pipeline, because a target may rerun many times:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
kl_log_verdicts(kl_read_verdicts(kl_newest_verdicts("qa", review = "annual-2026-qa")))
```

## 8. Keep a decision log that shows if it was altered

```{r}
kl_log_decision("Exclude test records from the intake extract", "approved",
                by = "Analyst A", basis = "Test records carry a fixed prefix",
                evidence = "WP-04 record filter", assurance = "self-reviewed",
                ref = "annual-2026")
kl_log_decision("Use 2024 police district boundaries", "approved",
                by = "Analyst A", reviewed_by = "Supervisor S",
                assurance = "peer-reviewed", ref = "annual-2026")
kl_decisions()[, c("seq", "what", "by", "assurance")]
kl_verify_log()
```

Each entry carries the hash (a fingerprint of its exact contents) of the
one before it. Edit, remove or reorder an earlier entry and
`kl_verify_log()` names the first one that no longer fits. Assurance levels
are checked too: anything above `self-reviewed` needs a named second person.

What the chain cannot catch by itself is someone rewriting the whole file,
or removing the newest entries. For that, record the head outside the
folder at milestones, such as when a report goes out:

```{r}
head <- kl_log_head()
kl_verify_log(expect_head = head)
```

Paste the head into the work papers or an email to a supervisor. Any later
check against it fails if the log was rewritten or cut short since. One
writer at a time: two people appending at the same moment on a shared drive
can break the chain.

## A note on version control

Git, the version control system, is free and open source, maintained by an
independent community; it runs entirely on your own machines and needs no
account with anyone. GitHub is one of several places people *host* Git
repositories, and using it is optional. When your office is
ready, this whole `knowledge/` folder goes into Git as it stands.

To start with no server at all, IT can create a *bare* repository (a Git
repository with no working files, used only to share) on the shared drive.
Each analyst clones it to their own machine, works there, and pushes back.
Don't work directly inside a repository that sits on the shared drive: network
drives and Git's working files don't mix well.

If the office wants what GitHub offers (a shared place to browse code, review
changes before they are merged, and track issues) on a server it controls,
two open-source options run entirely inside the network:

- **Forgejo** (<https://forgejo.org>), licensed GPLv3 or later. A community
  project; its trademarks and domains are held by Codeberg e.V., a German
  nonprofit association.
- **Gitea** (<https://about.gitea.com>), licensed MIT. Forgejo began as a fork
  of Gitea in 2022 and has developed separately since 2024. Gitea is
  company-backed (Gitea Ltd); a commercial edition is sold by its subsidiary,
  CommitGo.

Both are light enough for a modest internal machine and work with RStudio's
built-in Git pane. The repositories they hold are ordinary Git repositories
that can move to any other host later, so choosing one locks nothing in.
Either goes through your software vetting like any other tool.

A sensible order: a bare repository on the shared drive first, the
knowledge layer beside it, and a Forgejo or Gitea server once more than one
analyst is working on the same project.
